analysis.one_liner: Bans former members of Congress, senior executive appointees, and top generals from ever lobbying for foreign governments.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by Rep. Jared Golden and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, but never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill amends the Foreign Agents Registration Act to make it illegal for anyone who has served as a member of Congress, a senior political appointee, or a general or flag officer in the military to ever work as a paid agent of a foreign government [S2]. It also extends the existing one-year post-service restrictions on these officials so they apply indefinitely rather than for just one year [S2]. The rules would apply only to officials whose service ends after the bill becomes law [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who want foreign governments to hire American lobbyists through transparent, accountable channels rather than through former senators, cabinet officials, and generals cashing in on their government connections [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Adds a new section to the Foreign Agents Registration Act prohibiting anyone who served as a member of Congress, a senior political appointee, or a general or flag officer from registering as an agent of a foreign principal or serving in that role [S2].

Defines 'senior political appointee' broadly, covering presidential and vice-presidential appointees, noncareer Senior Executive Service members, and other confidential or policymaking positions in executive agencies [S2].

Amends the post-service conflict-of-interest provision in federal criminal law so the existing restrictions apply to these covered officials at any time after service, not just within the current one-year window [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Former senior officials and the lobbying and consulting firms that hire them to represent foreign governments would lose a lucrative career path. Foreign governments lose a favored route to influence [S2].

drawbacks.text: A permanent, lifetime ban is far broader than the current one-year cooling-off rule, and critics of such restrictions argue they can deter people from taking senior government jobs in the first place or from representing a foreign country in entirely legitimate capacities, such as trade negotiation or legal defense [S2].

A hard ban on registered foreign-agent work could push influence activity into unregistered channels, since the bill removes the very registration requirement that makes the work visible to the public [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real revolving-door problem: former top officials selling their access to foreign governments, often through firms that specialize in that trade. A lifetime ban is the bluntest possible instrument, and honest supporters would concede it goes further than the existing one-year rule and could have the side effect of driving some foreign-influence work out of the registered system entirely. On balance, the core idea — that people who held the public's trust should not profit from it on behalf of foreign powers — is widely shared, but the bill as written is a maximal version that never received any committee scrutiny or refinement.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Golden introduced the bill on April 30, 2024, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1] [S4].
One House Democrat cosponsored the bill; no other members of either party joined [S3].
The Judiciary Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died with the end of the 118th Congress [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lobbying and consulting firms that employ former officials to represent foreign governments keep the talent pipeline intact, and former members of Congress, senior appointees, and flag officers keep this career path open. The public gains nothing because the bill never advanced [S3] [S4].

for.name: Rep. Jared Golden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Congressional and Executive Foreign Lobbying Ban Act in the House on April 30, 2024 [S1] [S2].

for.name: 1 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill after it was introduced [S3].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction; bill referred there April 30, 2024
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — and it expired when the Congress ended [S4].

sides.party_line_note: The bill was so small — a single sponsor and one cosponsor, both Democrats — that neither party's position was ever tested; no member of the majority party signed on and the committee never considered it [S3] [S4].

industries.note: These firms build their business on hiring former members of Congress, cabinet-level appointees, and generals precisely for their connections, and a lifetime FARA ban would cut off their supply of marquee talent [S2]. Their gain from the bill dying is the public's loss of a transparency safeguard, since the registered-agent system is where foreign influence is supposed to be visible.

industries.industry: Former senior officials (members of Congress, senior appointees, flag officers)
industries.note: The bill would permanently bar these officials from a well-paid career path representing foreign principals, the single most lucrative use of their government connections. Their interest in keeping it open runs directly against the public's interest in closing the revolving door to foreign influence [S2].
